title: Smolov program review (from an hypertrophy standpoint)
summary: NH reviews the Smolov squat program purely from a hypertrophy angle. It will build big quads but concentrates tonnage on one lift, risks the knees and neglects hip hinges and the rest of the body, so it suits a deliberate 'sacrifice block' followed by maintaining the gains.
claims: Any program costing 80 dollars, like Kinobody's, is not worth buying
Strength programs also build muscle because building strength builds muscle, and powerlifters usually have huge quads naturals can learn from
Smolov needs a known 1RM, so lifters unused to maxing will plug in an inaccurate number and outgrow the program as their max technique improves
He doesn't know his 1RM and currently squats 375 for 6
Legs grow from minimalist training: heavy squats and deadlifts are simple but not easy
Heavy squats and deadlifts save time for naturals: they deliver big tonnage fast, leaving room for higher-volume upper body work
Programs need an acclimation period; throwing lifters into deep water in week one is a recipe for disaster
He is not a big proponent of stretching and doesn't find it very useful
Specialization programs put all eggs in one basket; bodybuilders train many movement patterns so the rest of the body will suffer
Progressing one lift while keeping others stable is a powerlifting mentality that doesn't suit bodybuilding
A specialization block can make sense if you have a big quad weak point to catch up
Heavy squats 4 days a week in the base cycle is more frequency than he could handle
Many people start these programs as novices or on big bulks, so their gains reflect noob gains and food rather than the program
Running Smolov at maintenance versus eating everything is night and day for leverage and recovery
That much knee flexion eats recovery so heavy pulls or even overhead pressing on top become doubtful
Squatting without hip hinges gives poor hamstring development, and lots of quad with weak hamstrings primes a knee injury
Many who think they fail mid-squat actually failed to build speed out of the hole; same for bench off the chest
Strength training waves tonnage up and down to peak, while bodybuilding wants stable tonnage that only dips slightly
If tonnage dips completely you either stopped training the body part or got injured
His philosophy is never fail a rep; failing means his calculations were off
Failing reps raises injury risk, kills you mentally and wrecks your volume afterwards; failing weekly means the program is wrong
3x4 at about 95% intensity is still rep work and a big quad hypertrophy block, with knee pain risk
Bodybuilders want stronger lifts because base strength allows more weight everywhere, more tonnage, and more tonnage makes muscles bigger
Getting stronger means bigger only if done within a program that promotes tonnage
After Smolov you can't keep feeding legs that tonnage, so expect some loss of size and strength
Using Smolov: run it occasionally as a 30-week sacrifice, protect your knees, keep some hip hinges, then maintain the bigger squat
He once curled every day with massive tonnage, biceps grew, and after cutting back he kept size and strength
Maintaining a specialized muscle needs less work than building it, but legs need far more maintenance tonnage than biceps
Smolov is more extreme than Squat Every Day or Widowmakers, which are more reasonable routes to bigger quads
exercises: builds quads but knee risk and concentrated tonnage
